```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 0.3)

# draws n full-width blank lines (margin to margin) for handwritten answers,
# as a single plot so spacing is deterministic; pair with fig.height = 0.3 * n
blank_lines <- function(n = 1) {
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, n), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    segments(0, n - i + 0.5, 1, n - i + 0.5, lwd = 1)
  }
}

# reserves blank work space (no ruled lines) for equation manipulation /
# show-your-work; pair with fig.height set to however much room is needed
blank_space <- function() {
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
  plot.new()
}
```

```{r key-helpers, include=FALSE}
ans_col <- rgb(200, 0, 130, maxColorValue = 255)
# redraws blank_table() so cells flagged TRUE in `ans` use the answer color
blank_table <- function(headers, body, col_widths = NULL,
                        header_height = 0.35, row_height = 0.5,
                        cex = 0.95, bold_rows = integer(0), ans = NULL) {
  nc <- length(headers); nr <- length(body)
  if (is.null(col_widths)) col_widths <- rep(1, nc)
  col_widths <- col_widths / sum(col_widths)
  cx <- c(0, cumsum(col_widths))
  h_total <- header_height + nr * row_height
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0), family = "serif")
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, h_total), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "",
       xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i")
  y <- h_total
  segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = 1.5)
  y <- y - header_height
  segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = 1.5)
  for (i in seq_len(nr)) {
    y <- y - row_height
    segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = if (i == nr) 1.5 else 0.5,
             col = if (i == nr) "black" else "grey70")
  }
  for (v in cx) segments(v, 0, v, h_total, lwd = 1)
  yh <- h_total - header_height / 2
  for (j in seq_len(nc)) text((cx[j] + cx[j + 1]) / 2, yh, labels = headers[[j]], font = 2, cex = cex)
  y <- h_total - header_height
  for (i in seq_len(nr)) {
    yc <- y - row_height / 2
    for (j in seq_len(nc)) {
      val <- body[[i]][[j]]
      is_ans <- !is.null(ans) && isTRUE(ans[[i]][[j]])
      if (!identical(val, "")) text((cx[j] + cx[j + 1]) / 2, yc, labels = val, cex = cex,
                                    font = if (i %in% bold_rows) 2 else 1,
                                    col = if (is_ans) ans_col else "black")
    }
    y <- y - row_height
  }
}
```

\ans{\textbf{Answer key.} Answers are in magenta.}


**NRES 746 -- Week 1, Lecture 2: Pseudocoding a Permutation Test**

&nbsp;


&nbsp;

**Instructions:** Work alone for about 5 minutes on Parts 1-2. Then get
together with your neighbor(s) and spend about 5 minutes on Part 3,
translating your pseudocode into actual R syntax **by hand, on paper**
(laptops and phones put away).

## Background: what is a permutation test?

In previous stats classes, you've seen tests for whether a sample's mean differed
from a known null distribution: e.g., a z-test, and a t-test.
These tests rely on knowing (or assuming) the shape
of the population distribution the data came from.

A **permutation test** drops that requirement. It's a *nonparametric*
(distribution-free) test: instead of simulating data from an assumed
distribution, we generate a null distribution for our test statistic by
**randomly reshuffling the labels** (e.g., treatment vs. control) on the
data we already have, over and over. If the group labels really don't
matter, shuffling them shouldn't change/reduce the expected
difference between group means very much. If the observed difference is
much larger than what typical reshufflings produce, that's evidence the
labels matter.

## Part 1: The scenario

Here's the scenario: pygmy short-horned lizards were sampled from a
cheatgrass-removal treatment area (trtA) and a nearby untreated control
area (Control). We want to know whether body mass differs between the
two groups.

```
   trtA:      175  168  168  190  156  181  182  175  174  179
   Control:   185  169  173  173  188  186  175  174  179  180
```

**1a.** What is the observed test statistic (the data summary 
we'll compare against the null distribution)?

\ans{The difference in mean body mass: $\bar x_{\text{trtA}} - \bar x_{\text{Control}} = 174.8 - 178.2 = -3.4$ (or its absolute value, 3.4).}

**1b.** Is the alternative hypothesis one-tailed or two-tailed ? Briefly explain why.

\ans{Two-tailed: the question is whether mass *differs*, with no direction predicted in advance.}

## Part 2: Write the pseudocode

**2.** In words, describe the algorithm you would need to
run a permutation test on this data. Think about: what gets shuffled, what
gets recomputed each time, how many times you repeat it, and how you turn
the result into a p-value.

\ans{Compute the observed difference in means. Then, many times (e.g. 10,000): shuffle the group labels at random across all 20 lizards, recompute the difference in means for the shuffled groups, and store it. The p-value is the fraction of stored differences at least as extreme as the observed one (in absolute value, for a two-tailed test).}

Flag any particular points of confusion that you'd like to come back to for discussion!

\ansbegin

```
permutation_test <- function(data, group, value, reps){
  labs <- unique(data[[group]])
  observed_dif <- mean(data[[value]][data[[group]] == labs[1]]) -
                  mean(data[[value]][data[[group]] == labs[2]])
  null_difs <- numeric(reps)
  for(i in 1:reps){
    shuffled_labels <- sample(data[[group]])
    null_difs[i] <- mean(data[[value]][shuffled_labels == labs[1]]) -
                    mean(data[[value]][shuffled_labels == labs[2]])
  }
  p_value <- mean(abs(null_difs) >= abs(observed_dif))
  return(p_value)
}
```

\ansend
